newsitem.title: USA: China sold Iran missile technology, report says.
newsitem.headline: China sold Iran missile technology, report says.

text.p: China recently sold Iran missile technology, advanced radar components and nearly 400 tons of chemicals used to produce nerve agents, the Washington Times reported on Thursday, citing the Central Intelligence Agency.

In an article ahead of a weekend meeting between U.S. President Bill Clinton and Chinese President Jiang Zemin, the newspaper said the reported transfer of missile-guidance components to Iran may violate Beijing's commitment to an international pact on curbing such sales.

In addition, some of the reported arms-technology transfers may violate a 1992 U.S. law that requires sanctions to be imposed on any nation exporting destabilising conventional weapons to Iran or Iraq, the newspaper said.

The State Department had no immediate comment on the report, which appeared as Secretary of State Warren Christopher was setting the stage for the Clinton-Jiang Zemin talks at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit meeting in Manila.

Citing what it called a top-secret October 2 CIA report titled "Arms Transfers to State Sponsors of Terrorism," the Washington Times said the China Precision Engineering Department had agreed in August to sell gyroscopes and other high-technology devices to Iran that could be used to build and test missile guidance components.

It also delivered in the summer nearly 400 metric tons of chemicals, including carbon sulfide, used to make nerve gas, and another chemical used in producing riot-control agents and tear gas, the paper quoted the CIA report as saying.
The CIA also reported the shipment of air defence gear and about 5,000 metric tons of other military equipment, possibly to upgrade Iran's Chinese-made anti-ship missiles, the Times said.
In Shanghai, Christopher praised what he called Chinese steps to improve civil rights and implored Beijing to seize an opportunity to build a new era of cooperation with the United States.
"As nuclear powers, permanent members of the U.N. Security Council and two of the world's biggest economies, we must lead" to promote global peace and prosperity, Christopher said.

The Clinton administration, eager to put ties with China on a more positive footing, has decided against imposing sanctions this year in several possible breaches of arms control pacts, including the sale of nuclear technology to Pakistan. Chinese leaders claimed they were unaware of the sale.
